Can you prove this theorem?

Theorem 6.2.2 (Hanson–Wright inequality). Let \(A\) be an \(n\times n\) matrix. Let \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) be a random vector with independent, mean-zero, subgaussian coordinates. Then, for every \(t\ge 0\),
\[
\mathbb{P}\!\left(\left|X^{\mathsf T}AX-\mathbb{E}[X^{\mathsf T}AX]\right|\ge t\right)
\le 2\exp\!\left[-c\min\!\left\{\frac{t^2}{K^4\lVert A\rVert_F^2},\frac{t}{K^2\lVert A\rVert}\right\}\right],
\]
where \(K=\max_i\lVert X_i\rVert_{\psi_2}\).

Theorem 4.7.1 (Covariance estimation). Let \(X\) be a subgaussian random vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). More specifically, assume that there exists \(K\ge 1\) such that
\[
\lVert\langle X,x\rangle\rVert_{\psi_2}\le K\lVert\langle X,x\rangle\rVert_{L^2}
\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n.\tag{4.29}
\]
Then, for every positive integer \(m\),
\[
\mathbb{E}\lVert\Sigma_m-\Sigma\rVert
\le CK^2\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{m}}+\frac{n}{m}\right)\lVert\Sigma\rVert.
\]

Lemma 8.3.14 (Dimension reduction). Let \(F\) be a finite class of Boolean functions on a domain \(\Omega\) with a probability measure \(\mu\). Assume that all functions in \(F\) are \(\varepsilon\)-separated, that is,
\[
\lVert f-g\rVert_{L^2(\mu)}>\varepsilon
\qquad\text{for all distinct }f,g\in F.
\]
If \(n\ge C\varepsilon^{-4}\log|F|\), then the empirical measure \(\mu_n\) satisfies, with probability at least \(0.99\),
\[
\lVert f-g\rVert_{L^2(\mu_n)}>\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
\qquad\text{for all distinct }f,g\in F.
\]
By definition of the empirical measure (Section 8.2.3), the population average is replaced by the sample average:
\[
\lVert f-g\rVert_{L^2(\mu_n)}
=\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl((f-g)(X_i)\bigr)^2\right)^{1/2},\tag{8.32}
\]
where \(X_i\) are independent, identically distributed copies of \(X\).

Can you prove this theorem?

Theorem 7.2.2 (Slepian inequality). Let \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) and \((Y_t)_{t\in T}\) be two mean-zero Gaussian processes. Assume that, for all \(t,s\in T\),
\[
\mathbb{E}X_t^2=\mathbb{E}Y_t^2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb{E}(X_t-X_s)^2\le\mathbb{E}(Y_t-Y_s)^2.\tag{7.3}
\]
Then \(\sup_{t\in T}X_t\) is stochastically dominated by \(\sup_{t\in T}Y_t\): for every \(\tau\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
\mathbb{P}\!\left\{\sup_{t\in T}X_t\ge\tau\right\}
\le\mathbb{P}\!\left\{\sup_{t\in T}Y_t\ge\tau\right\}.\tag{7.4}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\in T}X_t\le\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\in T}Y_t.\tag{7.5}
\]

Lemma 2.7.8 (Centering). Any subgaussian random variable \(X\) satisfies
\[
\lVert X-\mathbb{E}X\rVert_{\psi_2}\le C\lVert X\rVert_{\psi_2}.
